課程綱要.課程目標: 本課程原名「影像分析與寫作」，本年度授課者課程著重媒體與戲劇的分析與創意寫作，立意以「媒體藝術」與「表演藝術」作為應用人文與社會實踐的教學策略，引導學生在藝術創作的實踐中，學習人文運用的技巧以及社會實踐的意義。
課程綱要.授課內容:
本課程內容採工作坊形式，在三部分五段式教學中，按部就班引導學生瞭解並學習舞台劇獨幕劇與電影短片寫作的技巧，學生將在本學期中完成英文劇本3篇，並透過讀劇與全班分享。第一部分自第一至三段至，重點在於劇本寫組基本概念與練習，同學將透過經典閱讀認識戲劇結構與分景、空間與場景、對白與潛臺詞、角色人物等主要元素。第一部分的三階段課程結束前，同學將完成第一篇英文短劇寫作，長度以十分鐘為限。第四段教學將進入劇場空間，
第二部分以及四階段教學，將以改編為主軸，教學拉到劇場空間，運用劇場身體遊戲，建立學生對於戲劇結構、角色人物建立乃至人物與各類空間的關係，繼續進行劇本寫作練習。第二部分同樣以一個短劇寫作和讀劇作為終點。第三部分除了繼續以劇場空間為教學場域，主題則改以短片（動畫或偶戲）劇本書寫為主，介紹同學在集體合作之下，完成自己的劇本寫作，並以一個短片劇本為終結。

Acting Exercises for Non-Traditional Staging: Michael Chekhov Reimagined (Anjalee Deshpande Hutchison).

課程綱要.課程目標: The objective of this course is to develop students’ ability to read, analyze, and assess written texts in academic and professional contexts. We will explore the importance of reading in a wide range of activities, including independent critical thinking and social and political participation. The course is designed to equip students with the necessary reading skills for more advanced courses and their professional lives after college.
課程綱要.授課內容: Class activities will consist of short in-class readings, brief writing responses, and group work on questions related to the readings. Along with the in-class readings, students will be given study questions with analytical frameworks for thinking critically about each text. These handouts will also introduce new vocabulary and relevant historical and cultural background. Following each reading, class meetings will consist of independent writing responses or student-led discussions in pairs, groups, and as a class. The midterm and final exams will be in-class essays (closed book; no electronic devices; a print dictionary will be provided).

課程綱要.課程目標: This course aims to enhance your English oral proficiency, foster critical thinking, and cultivate the cultural awareness necessary for effective communication. Our in-class activities will consist of group presentations, small group discussions, and whole-class dialogue. The oral training is primarily text-based, though we will also incorporate online videos and film screenings. These diverse texts provide a foundation for you to learn how to identify core arguments, engage with them critically, and explore their significance within specific cultural and historical contexts. Over the semester, you will learn to refine your ability to structure arguments and articulate thoughts with clarity, all while reflecting on your own intellectual and emotional development. It is hoped that you will complete the course with the confidence to express your views persuasively in English, and that you will gain a broadened and less polarized worldview along with a sharpened sense of self-awareness.

課程綱要.課程目標: This course provides a space to strengthen your English speaking skills with particular attention to developing critical thinking and analytical ability in spoken language. In-class work will center on student-led group presentations and discussions, both in small groups and as a class, grounded in weekly assigned texts as well as related materials and issues that engaged students bring in. These texts are meant not only to enrich vocabulary but also to spark discussion and to draw us into the historical and socio-cultural significance of past and present events. Over the course of the semester, students are expected to practice speaking more effectively and persuasively in English, while also developing sensitivities to cultural and socio-historical contexts. At the same time, students will learn to identify the central arguments of individual articles, the perspectives that inform them, and the stakes at play. By engaging closely with these readings, students will be asked to develop their own arguments, questions, and critiques. A central aim of the course is to prepare students for the next level of academic and professional presentation.

課程綱要.課程目標: Comp History This course introduces freshmen to the basic skills of critical thinking required in the study of English literature, cultural studies, and critical theory. It does so through a dialectic analysis of key concepts in Western thought. We will examine the assumptions and premises or major topics regarding the function of poetry in society, with an emphasis on notions of property, possession, and individualism. We will see that poetry occupies a space of radical resistance to the dominant ideologies of any time period. Students are expected to complete readings at home and to bring questions to class (graded course component). The course also introduces students to the basics of how to occupy a college classroom by challenging the instructor and how to engage in argumentative writing (graded course component).
課程綱要.授課內容: At the heart of this experiment and theory and the history of ideas, we will engage with the seeming “inevitability” of contemporary global capitalism. We will question whether notions of labor, alienation, progress, inequality, freedom, and others are as obvious and necessary as they seem.

課程綱要.評量配分比重: Students must attend class having completed the readings. Students must bring questions on card to class each week. This activity and a writing activity every three weeks will amount to 50% of the grade. Another 20％ will be determined through an in-class midterm exam, through which students will be asked to define and identify several key terms discussed in the first half of the course, and to compose a very short essay (500 words). The final 30％ of the class will be determined through a final paper of 4-5 pages (double spaced, 12-point Times New Roman), which students will write by building on one of several provided essay topics or by determining their own topic with the Professor’s assistance.

課程綱要.課程目標: The objective of this course is to develop students’ oral presentation skills. The focus is on how to prepare and deliver effective presentations. In addition, students will learn how to ask informed, focused, and helpful questions as well as how to answer questions in academic and professional contexts.
課程綱要.授課內容:
Note: Students who have taken Professor Ding's 2023 Spring Oral Training (111學年第2學期) should avoid taking this course because it covers similar materials.
Class activities will be based on short readings and film screenings. Students will be given readings and study questions that introduce analytical frameworks for thinking critically about each text. In addition, students will be provided with handouts that introduce new vocabulary as well as relevant historical and cultural background. Following each reading or screening, class meetings will consist of student-led discussions in pairs, groups and/or as a class. The mid-term will consist of group presentations; the final exam will be an individual presentation followed by a question and answer period. All conversation in this course will be conducted in English.
Our topic this semester is failure. In class and as short homework assignments we will read excerpts from Judith Halberstam's The Queer Art of Failure. We will discuss it as we view films and read short fiction that dramatizes valuable failures and admirable losers. We will examine critically what counts as success and what doesn't, and why, and we will imagine other possible ways to determine value. In Halberstam’s words, we will explore how “failing, losing, forgetting, unmaking, undoing, unbecoming, not knowing may in fact offer more creative, more cooperative, more surprising ways of being in the world.”

課程綱要.評量配分比重: Grades will be calculated according to students’ weekly participation (40%), midterm presentation (15%), and the final presentation (25%). Attendance is mandatory: two unexcused absences are permitted; a third will result in a conference with the instructor. More than three absences are grounds for failing the class. Students must also come to class on time.

課程綱要.課程目標: In the course, students will expect to:  Develop a critical understanding of literary texts produced under the reign of Elizabeth I  Develop the historical/political mindset to interrogate the representations of Elizabeth I in the context of early modern queenship  To cultivate and enhance the skill set of research and project-making via both in-class activities and take-home assignment
課程綱要.授課內容:
*本課程為英文系高年級(三、四年級)專業文學課程，並以全英文授課。非此設定範圍但欲選修該課程的同學(含本系及外系同學)，請參與開學第一堂課，並在課後與授課老師集體面談。若符合修課標準，會視情況核發選課密碼卡。若有其他問題，請直接來信授課老師。If you need the passcode, you MUST attend the first meeting.
For centuries Elizabeth I has attracted much attention from historians via several distinct public images: she is the disavowed daughter of Henry VIII and the ‘great whore’ Anne Boleyn, the loving sister of Edward VI, the religious rivals of Mary Tudor and Mary of Scots, and of course, the virgin Queen, and literatures converging on these images have testified to the golden age of England in the sixteenth century, from Philip Sidney to John Lyly, from William Shakespeare to Edmund Spenser. How do we come to terms with Elizabeth’s omnipresence in literature (particularly as a female ruler)? What does it say about the interplay between literature and politics in the Renaissance? In what way can we think of the queen as a major influencer of sixteenth-century England? With these core questions in mind, this course seeks to read a cluster of important literary texts centering on the political representation of Elizabeth I. The entire course will be taught in English and is suitable for those who are interested in the history, culture, and literature of the early modern period. Former knowledge in English Studies 1 is preferred but not required.
數個世紀以來，英國女皇伊莉莎白一世一直是歷史學家熱切關注的對象；她的形象多元而富有爭議：她是亨利八世與「大淫婦」安妮・博林的女兒、是愛弟如命的姊姊、是瑪麗・都鐸與瑪麗・斯圖雅特這兩位宗教政敵的對手、更是鼎鼎大名的童貞女王。而圍繞這些形象所形成的文學作品—從菲利普・席德尼、約翰・萊利、到莎士比亞與史賓賽—共同見證了英國十六世紀的黃金時代。站在現代的角度，我們該如何理解伊莉莎白在文學作品中的各種鏡像呢？這些現象如何揭示文學與文藝復興時期政治之間的互動關係？我們又可以從哪些面向思考她身為十六世紀英格蘭最重要的媒體影響者？本課程將以這些核心問題為出發點，細讀一系列聚焦於伊莉莎白一世政治形象的文學作品。

In this course we will read a cluster of key texts that shape the contour of the English literary canon against the backdrop of the rise of the British Empire in the early periods (up to the end of the 17th century). We will cover some of the most prominent literary genres informed by the linguistic transformation from Middle English to Early Modern English, such as frame narrative, romance, fabliau, drama, sonnet, and metaphysical poetry. By reading these texts, students are expected to not only gain a more diverse, comprehensive understanding of the changing nature of “Englishness,” but also develop a critical sense of individual texts pertaining to their historical backgrounds and contexts.
本課程將閱讀一系列影響英國早期文學正典形成的重要文本，並將其置於大英帝國初期興起的歷史背景下加以探討。我們將涵蓋十四至十七世紀間許多重要的文學體裁--包括框架敘事、羅曼史、諷刺寓言詩、戲劇、十四行詩與形而上詩--並閱讀從喬叟到莎士比亞等經典作家的代表作品。透過閱讀這些文本，學生不僅能更全面且多元地理解「英國性」隨時代變遷的樣貌，也將學習如何批判性地閱讀文本與其所處的歷史語境。本課程全程以英文授課。

課程綱要.課程目標: Over the past two decades, LGBT rights movements have expanded rapidly across much of the world. With the hegemonic rise of the “global queer” as the new normal, a pressing question emerges for queers in Third World Asia: how can this positionality be rethought in light of shifting geopolitical alignments? This course takes up that question through the frameworks of Inter-Asia Cultural Studies and transnational queer critique. The course is divided into three units. We begin by examining sex, gender, and sexuality as sites of Foucauldian knowledge production in both Anglophone and Inter-Asian contexts, establishing the course’s materialist analytic approach. Next, we turn a critical lens on the figure of the global LGBT, analyzing how queer liberalism—entangled with the non-profit, prison, and academic industrial complexes—advances through processes of homonationalism, homocapitalism, and transnational gender governance. 課程綱要.課程目標: This course introduces students to the historical formations of inter-Asia cultural studies as movements, thoughts, problematics, and praxis to foreground the trajectories of inter-Asia processes. This entails our investigation of disciplinary demarcations cohered in colonial-imperial-national divides out of which cultural studies emerge, while also critically challenging the boundaries of knowledge production and social practices. Implicated in the process, we will also explore how inter-Asia comes forward and reorients our problematics about imperialism, cold wars, and decolonization long overshadowed by the Anglo-American axis. Drawing on trans-local critical thought-resources in and as a global making process, we will also explore inter-Asia methods with which to problematize “Asia,” to inquire into “inter-Asia subjectivity,” and to experiment with creative and critical space for the emergence of renewed social and cultural movements.
